title: How Your Brain Makes Decisions
desc: Stay, or go? One sheet of paper, two columns, and a decision that won't make itself. In this calm, sourced deep dive we follow one imagined person, Mara, through one long evening at her kitchen table, and use her choice to explore how your brain really makes decisions: fast and slow thinking, why feelings are part of reason (Damasio's patient Elliot), the shortcuts your mind takes, anchoring and framing, the pull of defaults, too much choice and the hungry judge debate, when to trust your gut, the brain signals before a choice (Libet), choice blindness and the reasons we invent afterwards, other people's influence, why we misjudge future feelings, how risk feels, regret, and a few gentle tools for choosing well, including what a coin flip can tell you. Every claim comes from named studies, with the doubts left in. At the end there is a slow, gentle wind-down, so you can listen until you drift off.

plan: b01: hook (Mara at the kitchen table, two columns: stay / go) + 'Tonight, we'll explore' list; the myth of 35,000 decisions a day; open loop: can a coin help (paid off b16)
b02: two speeds: Frederick 2005 cognitive reflection test (lily pads, widgets); Stanovich & West 2000; Kahneman 2011; Müller-Lyer 1889; Melnikoff & Bargh 2018 caveat
b03: feelings: Damasio 1994 Elliot and the appointment dates; somatic markers; Bechara et al. 1997 card decks; Maia & McClelland 2004 doubt; Schwarz & Clore 1983 weather and Lucas & Lawless 2013
b04: heuristics: Tversky & Kahneman 1974; availability 1973 (letter K); Lichtenstein et al. 1978; Linda 1983; Hertwig & Gigerenzer 1999; Goldstein & Gigerenzer 2002 recognition
b05: anchoring: wheel of fortune 1974 (25 vs 45); Strack & Mussweiler 1997 Gandhi (67 vs 50); Englich et al. 2006 dice and sentences; Many Labs 2014; Epley & Gilovich 2001; consider the opposite 2000
b06: framing: Tversky & Kahneman 1981 (72% / 78%); losses loom larger 1979; McNeil et al. 1982 survival vs mortality; Levin & Gaeth 1988 lean vs fat
b07: defaults: Johnson & Goldstein 2003; Knetsch 1989 mugs and chocolate; Samuelson & Zeckhauser 1988 status quo bias; Spranca, Minsk & Baron 1991 omission bias

b08: too much choice: Simon 1956 satisficing; Schwartz et al. 2002 maximisers; Iyengar & Lepper 2000 jam and Scheibehenne 2010; Chernev et al. 2015; Danziger et al. 2011 parole judges with Weinshall-Margel & Shapard 2011 and Glöckner 2016
b09: the gut: Klein 1998 firefighters; Chase & Simon 1973 chess; Kahneman & Klein 2009; Meehl 1954 and Grove et al. 2000; Wilson & Schooler 1991 jam; Wilson et al. 1993 posters
b10: who decides: Libet 1983; Soon et al. 2008 (~60%); Schurger, Sitt & Dehaene 2012; Dijksterhuis 2006 and failed replications (Acker 2008, Nieuwenstein 2015)
b11: our reasons: Johansson et al. 2005 choice blindness (13%); Hall et al. 2010 jam and tea; Hall et al. 2012 moral survey; Nisbett & Wilson 1977 stockings; Gazzaniga's interpreter
b12: other people: Asch 1951; Bond & Smith 1996; Salganik, Dodds & Watts 2006 music market; Galton 1907 ox; Janis 1972 groupthink

b13: forecasting feelings: Gilbert et al. 1998 impact bias; psychological immune system; Schkade & Kahneman 1998 focusing illusion; Gilbert & Ebert 2002 reversible choices; Gilbert et al. 2009 surrogation
b14: how risk feels: Slovic 1987 dread and unknown; Finucane et al. 2000 affect heuristic; Gigerenzer 2004 dread risk and road deaths; the quiet risks of staying
b15: regret: Gilovich & Medvec 1995 actions vs inactions; Medvec, Madey & Gilovich 1995 bronze vs silver; Read & van Leeuwen 1998 snacks; Read, Loewenstein & Kalyanaraman 1999 films
b16: tools: Grossmann & Kross 2014 Solomon's paradox; premortem (Klein 2007, Mitchell, Russo & Pennington 1989); Lord, Lepper & Preston 1984; Levitt 2021 coin flips (pays off b01)
b17: Mara's morning (sleeps on it, asks separately, premortem, coin in the air) + takeaways + callback to the two columns
b18: guided wind-down + end segment teasing What Stress Really Does to Your Brain
